name: Component Availability

claims.claim_text: Whether an integrated part can be bought in production quantity, rather than its electrical merit, often decides whether it can be designed in: a distributor showing five units in stock is useless for a build of 10,000 when the factory lead time is 40 weeks.
claims.quote_verbatim: they might have five in stock at Mouser or something, but you know, that doesn't help you when you want to build 10,000 of them and there's a 40 week lead time
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Substituting an unobtainable part propagates through a design rather than being a local swap; replacing a 10-cent chip that cannot be sourced with a 50-cent alternative forces changes to the surrounding circuitry and repeated BOM rework to recover cost.
claims.quote_verbatim: Oh, I love that chip. It's only 10 cents, but I can't get it. So I'm going to have to use the 50 cent chip. And then that flows on and changes the rest of your design.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Volume buyers concentrate purchasing on distributors that actually hold stock, since guaranteed availability outweighs catalogue breadth for parts needed in thousands.
claims.quote_verbatim: We're buying parts and we get them from Digikey and stuff like that because they're available.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Distributor selection during a shortage turns on stock position rather than brand: a distributor with no parts wins no business regardless of its name, and buyers will accept a higher unit price from whoever can actually ship.
claims.quote_verbatim: It doesn't matter to me what you're called if you have decent prices and you have availability, which is so much of a bigger deal these days.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: When components are in short supply the purchasing decision inverts, with unit price becoming secondary to whether the part can be obtained at all.
claims.quote_verbatim: Price isn't that much. It's can you get the parts, really?
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A part manufactured by many independent vendors is effectively immune to stock-out; the 555 timer, second-sourced by numerous manufacturers, can always be bought somewhere unless a designer insists on one specific brand's version.
claims.quote_verbatim: Very readily available. That's one part you'll never be stuck with.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: LED Designs, Last Minute Designs and Board Designs

claims.claim_text: Extended part-research phases can be self-defeating, because availability and pricing data go stale over the weeks spent gathering them and the selected parts may already be unobtainable by the time the search finishes.
claims.quote_verbatim: I've got to spend a month researching parts. Great. Yeah. And then by the time you finish that, they're all out of date and they can't get them anymore.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: LED Designs, Last Minute Designs and Board Designs

claims.claim_text: Reusable modular PCB-level building blocks tend to break down in practice partly because they carry parts the reusing designer cannot obtain easily or cheaply, on top of form-factor, power and voltage mismatches.
claims.quote_verbatim: it uses a part that you can't get now or they can't get easily or cheaply
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: NASA, WOTW & Modular Design - The NASA Nostalgia

claims.claim_text: Designing around the passives and transistors an assembly house already keeps loaded on its pick-and-place machines or in stock shortens build time and avoids sourcing risk, and is usually worth a small unit-cost penalty.
claims.quote_verbatim: then, you know, it pays to use that, pays to design that in, even if it might cost a little bit more
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Bob Widlar, Electronic Design, FIRST Robotics - Monday, Meta Monday

claims.claim_text: Distributor choice for small orders is driven by delivery speed as well as price and stock; Mouser ships from a warehouse near Dallas, so US customers using even the cheapest ground option often receive orders the following day.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm partial to Mauser because they are overnight shipping. Even if you pay for ground, they're located up near Dallas.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeff Keyzer - Comical Keyzer Comes a-Callin'

claims.claim_text: Tying an open hardware platform to a single silicon vendor exposes every downstream design to that vendor's supply position; the Arduino's dependence on Atmel microcontrollers left derivative products unable to source parts until the software was ported to other microcontroller families.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm designing something around the Atmel in the Arduino factory. You can't get the parts. It's a real problem.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeff Keyzer and Jeremy Blum - Audacious Arduino Arguments

claims.claim_text: For a new analog application many op amps typically meet the specification, so selection is decided by cost, availability and package type rather than by performance alone.
claims.quote_verbatim: it might come down to cost, cost availability, you know, package type, package size
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Op amps, Microchips & Mergers - Narquois Nerd Nescience - Narquois Nerd Nescience

claims.claim_text: Distributors outside the largest markets hold progressively less local stock and ship from regional hubs, so an Australian buyer ordering from Farnell may wait for goods routed from Singapore even when the part shows as available.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're holding less and less local stock and it's got to come from Singapore
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: No distributor stocks the whole component universe; catalogue depth is tiered, with Digi-Key deeper than regional distributors and the Shenzhen component markets deeper still on price and sometimes on availability.
claims.quote_verbatim: So, they can't carry everything. There's just too many parts
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A part can become unbuildable without being discontinued, because another buyer clears out distributor and factory stock, leaving the designer stranded on a current production part.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's not obsolete anymore, but some bastard's gone and sucked up all the stock, you know?
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Component selection commonly begins with a parametric search on distributor websites, restricting candidates to parts that can actually be purchased from Digi-Key or Mouser before any electrical evaluation.
claims.quote_verbatim: We go do our parametric search and we use the chips that we can actually buy on DigiKey and Mouser.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Øyvind Janbu - Feracious Fabless Facilitator

claims.claim_text: Checking distributor stock as the first step of design is practised in large companies as well as small ones, because prototype schedules measured in weeks collapse if the chosen part cannot be delivered.
claims.quote_verbatim: You look for what's available because you need a prototype next week. And, you know, and if you can't get the part, you're screwed.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Øyvind Janbu - Feracious Fabless Facilitator

claims.claim_text: Restricting a design to components anyone can buy on the open market in single quantities is what makes it self-buildable, a constraint that distinguishes hobbyist-reproducible hardware from designs relying on parts sold only under volume contracts.
claims.quote_verbatim: You could go and buy the components. They were all freely available components
claims.speaker: Eben Upton
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eben Upton - Morbus Moilsome MakerFaire

claims.claim_text: Semiconductor vendors publish an aggressively priced headline part with minimal peripherals and charge steeply for the variant with the feature actually required, so a 25-cent 32-bit microcontroller can become a $2 part once a 12-bit rather than 10-bit ADC is needed.
claims.quote_verbatim: oh, a 10-bit ADC isn't enough for me. I need to go to a 12-bit. Well, see you later. You're up at $2 now.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Loading a complete BOM into a distributor account lets a repeat build be re-ordered in minutes at the correct quantities and part numbers, which for small production runs can justify buying everything from one, more expensive, distributor.
claims.quote_verbatim: went to the trouble to put my bomb into DigiKey. And now I just go order 200.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Ceramic capacitors & High end scopes - Kempt Kickstarter Kakorrhaphiophobia

claims.claim_text: A stored distributor BOM reports live stock against every line before the order is placed, surfacing shortages at the point of ordering rather than after the money is committed.
claims.quote_verbatim: it tells you live in the bomb whether or not I have stock
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Ceramic capacitors & High end scopes - Kempt Kickstarter Kakorrhaphiophobia

claims.claim_text: Poor part selection can strand a programme after prototypes are built: a military sonar project reached a multi-million-dollar prototype PCB whose components could no longer be sourced, leaving the team to patch hardware together purely to pass a customer milestone.
claims.quote_verbatim: we've already produced the prototype, the massive prototype PCB and we can't get the parts anymore because the previous designer designed it poorly
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Distribution, Wozniak & Robots - Early Eight-bit Endgame

claims.claim_text: High-churn consumer product lines such as PC motherboards, which turn over roughly every six months, set their next design around whichever chips can be obtained at what price that week rather than around a fixed architecture.
claims.quote_verbatim: oh, what chip can we get this week? You know, that's what we're going to design our next run for
claims.episode_title: eReaders, datasheets & board assembly - Yearly Yeasty Yapping

claims.claim_text: Availability churns on a timescale of months, so a schematic revisited after a short interval typically requires re-selecting converter and charger ICs and re-running the whole BOM search for alternates on cost and stock.
claims.quote_verbatim: Oh, this DC to DC converter is not available anymore. Oh, it was available two months ago.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Layout, CAD & Raspberry Pi - Kedogenous Kinetic Knowledge

claims.claim_text: Deliberate second-sourcing of another vendor's catalogue is a commercial strategy built on that vendor's delivery failures, offering customers an alternate supply for parts they cannot reliably obtain from the original manufacturer.
claims.quote_verbatim: part of the reason we did second sourcing is because it serves a need out there
claims.speaker: Brett Fox
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brett Fox and Dr Jeroen Fonderie - Device Doubling Decretum

claims.claim_text: A supplier's delivery record persists as a design constraint long after the underlying problem is addressed, because engineers who have designed in a part and then been unable to buy it carry the professional consequences and avoid that supplier on later projects.
claims.quote_verbatim: You're designing their part and then you find you can't get it, you know, and you're screwed. And that makes you look bad as a design engineer.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brett Fox and Dr Jeroen Fonderie - Device Doubling Decretum

claims.claim_text: The economics of custom silicon are set against a distribution catalogue offering hundreds of thousands of characterised, tested parts at roughly a dollar each, which is why building a bespoke device rarely competes with buying a 50-cent microcontroller.
claims.quote_verbatim: you go on DigiKey, how many hundreds of thousands of parts are there for every conceivable application?
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brett Fox and Dr Jeroen Fonderie - Device Doubling Decretum

claims.claim_text: Part choices in large organisations are frequently made outside engineering, with purchasing departments overriding selections on the basis of component availability or supplier relationships.
claims.quote_verbatim: oftentimes purchasing makes decisions because of part availability
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Mars, System Design & NAND - Mercurial Mars Mission

claims.claim_text: Accepting an electrically sub-optimal component that is in stock is often the correct engineering choice over a better part that has a questionable supplier or cannot be obtained.
claims.quote_verbatim: You'll use a non-optimal part that you can get over a, you know, over a better part, which, you know, might have a questionable supplier, or that you can't get.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: PCB Mills, SDR and Oscilloscopes - Flaunting Furbelow Fanciness

claims.claim_text: Some components are not sold in one-off quantities at all, so incremental demand forces the purchase of a whole reel; an extra 1,000-piece reel at $4 per part can be required to satisfy a single additional unit of demand.
claims.quote_verbatim: I have to buy an extra reel of 1,000 components at $4 a pop
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Discussing Innovation and the Future with Mike Ossmann - Fiesty Festivus Futurology

claims.claim_text: A small board vendor moving to a newer FPGA generation waits not only for density and price to be right but for supply to be loose enough that much larger customers are not consuming the entire allocation.
claims.quote_verbatim: And the availability is such that I'm not banging heads with a lot bigger customers that can buy up everything and parts on location, things like that.
claims.speaker: Dave Vandenbout
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dave Vandenbout - Xceptional XESS Xenagogue

claims.claim_text: The worst point at which to discover a supply problem is mid-build, when the assembly house reports it has run out of a part that is no longer in stock and carries a 16-week lead time.
claims.quote_verbatim: We've run out of parts. And then they're not in stock. Oh. Yeah. Right. Yeah. It's only 16 week lead time.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Spacing Out On Space - Dave's Dongle Designing

claims.claim_text: For niche production volumes in the thousands, one workable approach is to plan the whole project around parts confirmed in stock at several independent distributors, treating multi-distributor stock as a precondition for designing a part in.
claims.quote_verbatim: So you plan your entire project. Around what you can get in stock.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Spacing Out On Space - Dave's Dongle Designing

claims.claim_text: Paying several times the normal unit price to a distributor that has stock is rational for a small manufacturer, because the premium is small against the cost of a stalled build and a missed delivery commitment.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'll pay $5 a chip. Instead of $1. But you know. As long as I can get it.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Spacing Out On Space - Dave's Dongle Designing

claims.claim_text: Buying long-lead components up front, before contracts with a manufacturing partner are finalised, pre-empts the delay introduced by the partner's own purchasing cycle, by which time the parts may have gone out of stock.
claims.quote_verbatim: And by the time they do that, oops, sorry, that, that, that parts out of stock. So you've got to preempt that.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Spacing Out On Space - Dave's Dongle Designing

claims.claim_text: Minimising distinct BOM line items is a design goal for kit and small-batch products, because every line item adds kitting labour and one more part that can become unobtainable.
claims.quote_verbatim: the number one thing that I wish I had done a better job of when I did the initial design is just using a fewer line items in the bomb
claims.episode_title: MightyHohm For The Holidays - Kaiser Keyzer's Kits

claims.claim_text: For a long-lived low-volume product, the loss of a component is usually what forces a redesign, since no other pressure is strong enough to justify reopening a design that still sells.
claims.quote_verbatim: I feel like probably the defining moment will be when a component is no longer available. That's when you say, oh, right now I've got to go work on this thing again.
claims.episode_title: MightyHohm For The Holidays - Kaiser Keyzer's Kits

claims.claim_text: Deferring component purchase until manufacturing begins is a common failure for low-volume projects, since parts that were listed at design time can be entirely unavailable, even in quantities of ten or a hundred, by the time the build is scheduled.
claims.quote_verbatim: they said they didn't buy the parts up front. And then by the time the manufacturing came around, it was like, Nope, those aren't, those aren't available anymore.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Supply Chain Woes And Wares - Nonplussed Neotechnic Nithing

claims.claim_text: Buying full reels ahead of demand ties up substantial working capital, with a single reel of resistors costing on the order of $4,000 and reels of 2,500 ICs bought at a time, and even that buffer is eventually consumed without warning.
claims.quote_verbatim: I ordered my, you know, $4,000 reel of resistors last time. Yes. I ordered a 2,500 reel of these chips
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Supply Chain Woes And Wares - Nonplussed Neotechnic Nithing

claims.claim_text: Low-volume turnkey assemblers restrict designs to their own stocked catalogue and waive the placement fee for in-house passives, while charging a placement fee for any component the customer supplies from outside.
claims.quote_verbatim: Whereas if you, if you bring in an outside part, there's a placement fee.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Questioning Everyday Prototyping - Verrucose Vehicle Vitilitigation

claims.claim_text: Local component availability is a function of trade access rather than technology: designers in Yugoslavia in the 1980s travelled roughly 1,000 kilometres to Munich to buy parts that are now sold domestically.
claims.quote_verbatim: At that time, I had to travel to Munich 1,000 kilometers.
claims.speaker: Voja Antonic
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Voja Antonic - Gerontogenous Galaksija Genesis

claims.claim_text: A design handed to a contract manufacturer should already have its part availability resolved, including any equivalent-part substitutions, because post-handoff changes are where the contract manufacturer earns its margin.
claims.quote_verbatim: you need to be very confident when you send it out to a CM because anything else, that's how they're making their margins
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Inspirations and Aspirations - Recanting Rocket Rationale

claims.claim_text: Relaunching a discontinued product line built on older analog ICs such as the 8038 function generator and bucket-brigade delay devices requires partial redesign, because the surviving catalogue dictates what compromises are possible.
claims.quote_verbatim: So there will be some compromises and some redesigns just based on the parts that are available.
claims.speaker: Fran Blanche

claims.claim_text: A part listed by a distributor is not necessarily promptly deliverable; catalogue presence and lead time are separate questions, and a part orderable at the push of a button may still be weeks away.
claims.quote_verbatim: even that's available from DigiKey, but it's a matter of lead time and stuff like that
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A distributor's review of a BOM validates sourceability, shipping times and lead-time normality, and should not be mistaken for validation that the circuit works.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's like, is it sourceable? Are you going to get screwed on your shipping times? Is it stuff, you know, is, is the lead times normal?
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Three Hundred Down, Three Hundred To Go

claims.claim_text: Releasing new part numbers faster than a fab and test operation can support them produces chronic supply failure; Maxim introduced around 500 new devices a year in the 1990s and could not ship many of them.
claims.quote_verbatim: So Maxim were coming out with 500 chips every year, which was a plus. That was like the, that was a slow year, you know, 500 new chips. And that was one of the reasons why they couldn't ship it.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Quoted lead times of around 50 weeks were reported for parts from suppliers with severe supply problems, a delay long enough to make a designed-in part effectively unavailable for a product cycle.
claims.quote_verbatim: That'll be 50 weeks lead time, sir.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A specialised variant of an otherwise common part, such as a microcontroller with an integrated LCD driver supporting an unusual segment count, may be absent from distribution simply because distributors decline to stock low-turnover variants rather than because it is discontinued.
claims.quote_verbatim: But in reality, it's just in distribution. They just don't stock these things.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Distributor listings showing a few hundred units shippable immediately typically carry a substantial price premium relative to normal supply.
claims.quote_verbatim: 293 can ship immediately. And you'll pay through the nose for them.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: For products intended for sale rather than experimentation, off-the-shelf integrated parts that are already characterised over temperature win on time to market against discrete implementations, provided they can be bought in quantity.
claims.quote_verbatim: to use these off-the-shelf chips that are already proven and characterized, you know, over temperature. It's just – yeah, there really isn't any contest.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A quoted lead time is only an estimate until goods are physically received, since natural disasters and other disruptions can extend delivery after an order is accepted.
claims.quote_verbatim: until you put that order in and even after you put that order, until you have the parts in your hands, you don't know what the true league time is
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Application processors aimed at low-cost consumer tablets turn over fast enough that a chipset can be unbuyable roughly two years after launch, forcing single-board computer vendors to maintain several hardware generations around successive chipsets.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's been on the market for two years, and the chip's gone
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Reports that a major distributor is out of an entire component category are usually overstated; ceramic capacitor shortages appeared as gaps at particular case size and voltage combinations rather than across the whole catalogue.
claims.quote_verbatim: Searching for a certain size and voltage, it may be true.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: During a passive component shortage prices rise noticeably and designers searching on specific part numbers should expect to re-evaluate the requirement and select a different part rather than wait for the original.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're searching for specific part numbers, you're going to have to do a little bit of reevaluation and find a new part
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Filter design tools expose the resistor and capacitor E-series as a selectable input because the chosen series directly determines how difficult the resulting component values will be to obtain.
claims.quote_verbatim: because that resistor series, capacitor series, because that basically determines how hard the component will be to get, right?

claims.claim_text: Accepting weaker performance from an amplifier already held in inventory can be the right engineering trade when the application's requirement is modest, since it avoids adding another part to stock.
claims.quote_verbatim: it allows you to avoid having to stock a new amplifier, then fantastic
claims.speaker: Matt Duff

claims.claim_text: Sourcing low-cost parts from consumer marketplaces carries a stock reliability penalty as well as a quality one: listings frequently cannot be fulfilled, and lots of a hundred warrant incoming inspection.
claims.quote_verbatim: the downsides though of AliExpress is they often won't have it in stock
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Multilayer ceramic capacitors reached lead times of roughly 72 weeks, long enough that designing one in without checking supply could make a product milestone unreachable.
claims.quote_verbatim: multi-layer ceramic capacitors for whatever reason had like a 72 week lead time
claims.speaker: Scott Miller

claims.claim_text: A BOM health risk assessment screens every line against component databases to flag parts that are not recommended for new designs, approaching end of life, single-sourced, or carrying long lead times, so those decisions can be corrected before they are locked in.
claims.quote_verbatim: we can look at any component and be like, Hey, you know, that one's not recommended for new designs, or that's going to be end of life, or this is available only from one supplier, uh, or it's got a really long lead time
claims.speaker: Scott Miller

claims.claim_text: Global available quantity is a graded criterion in supply risk scoring: a manufacturer part number with only a handful of units in worldwide inventory is materially riskier than one with millions, independent of its lifecycle status.
claims.quote_verbatim: So one is what's the global, um, availability of that component? Are there only two parts available or are there hundreds of thousands or millions or tens of millions available?
claims.speaker: Scott Miller

claims.claim_text: Identifying footprint-compatible cross-references and listing them as an approved vendor list gives the factory permitted drop-in substitutes, removing the sole-source dependency that arises when only one manufacturer part number is specified.
claims.quote_verbatim: are there crosses, um, that are say footprint compatible so that you could do an approved vendor list so that if the factory can find the part you specified, that's awesome. But if they can't, then here's like five other ones that you can just drop in
claims.speaker: Scott Miller

claims.claim_text: The recommended point for a supply risk review is roughly 80 percent through development, once the prototype functions, because early sourcing decisions cast long shadows but the BOM must exist before it can be graded.
claims.quote_verbatim: usually at that 80% point, once you've got the prototype functioning, that's an awesome time to do a bomb health risk assessment
claims.speaker: Scott Miller

claims.claim_text: Current distributor stock is a poor basis for a multi-year product, so sourcing decisions should be made against a forward risk profile rather than what happens to be listed at the moment of design.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't, you can't necessarily depend on what's in distribution right now. You have to look further out.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Designing around genuinely multi-sourced components, or failing that around parts stocked by several distributors, is the standard defence against supply interruption, though simultaneous clearance of stock across every distributor can still defeat it.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're smart, you'll try and design your, uh, product around, uh, something that has multiple sources. Or if you can't, at least, you know, it's in stock from multiple suppliers.

claims.claim_text: A board respin cannot be executed on a 24-hour timescale unless the components are already on hand, making local parts inventory the limiting factor in emergency rework.
claims.quote_verbatim: And you can't spin it in 24 hours, really, you know, unless you already had all the parts and everything else.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Withholding service parts is a lever manufacturers use to force replacement purchases; independent repair firms handling equipment such as endoscopes found spare components no longer supplied, obliging hospitals to buy new units.
claims.quote_verbatim: they were going over the price to fix these endoscopes and how parts weren't being made available anymore. So they had, so the hospitals would have to buy new ones.
claims.speaker: Louis Rossmann
claims.episode_title: Right To Repair with Louis Rossmann

claims.claim_text: Locating an ideal component is only the first hurdle; the immediate follow-up checks are whether it can be bought at all and whether its price is acceptable, since an otherwise perfect part may be sold out worldwide.
claims.quote_verbatim: And then there's that moment where you find the absolute ideal chip, and then you nervously say, A, is it available? B, is it affordable?
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison
claims.episode_title: LEDs and EVs with Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: Component library download counts follow a strong Pareto distribution, with roughly 20 percent of parts accounting for about 80 percent of downloads, which makes download frequency a usable proxy for identifying the jellybean part in a category.
claims.quote_verbatim: you'll definitely see that 20% of parts dominate 80% of the downloads
claims.speaker: Natasha Baker
claims.episode_title: Footprints and Symbols with Natasha Baker

claims.claim_text: Publishing schematics does not by itself make a product repairable if the components in them cannot be purchased or are serialised to the original unit.
claims.quote_verbatim: So even if Apple actually released the schematics, if you can't buy the parts or the serialized, well, no, you're screwed.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Price and availability data captured at schematic entry are stale by the time a product ships, because a design cycle of around nine months is long enough for both to change completely.
claims.quote_verbatim: the design cycle could be like nine months or something. It's like, oh yeah, it was a great price and availability nine months ago
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A more durable sourcing signal than a stock snapshot is a supplier score built on historical on-time delivery performance, which survives the design cycle better than a spot availability figure.
claims.quote_verbatim: you could start to look at things like, uh, what is the vendor score in terms of like on-time deliveries
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Distributor in-stock indicators are not reliable, with parts advertised as available proving not to be once an order is placed, so the flag should be treated as a claim to be confirmed rather than a guarantee.
claims.quote_verbatim: they promote that they have parts and then they do not
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Buying on lowest price alone from unfamiliar sources is a risk many engineers only learn to weigh after being burned, which is why filtering distributor search results to in-stock parts from known suppliers has become routine.
claims.quote_verbatim: so maybe if I've been burned enough times, I'll, I'll think twice
claims.speaker: Stephen Craig

claims.claim_text: Obtainability is part of the definition of a jellybean component: a part that can no longer be bought ceases to qualify regardless of how standard its function is.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you can't get it anymore, it no longer becomes jelly bean.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Even at build volumes in the tens of units, consultants work backup alternatives into the design phase, since a single hard-to-get component can stop the boards being built at all.
claims.quote_verbatim: you try to work your way around the design phase, such as to have some backup plan
claims.speaker: Florin Of Voltlog
claims.episode_title: YouTube to Consulting with Florin of Voltlog

claims.claim_text: Defence work commonly required three qualified parts from three different vendors for a given BOM position, so that any of them could be substituted into production without requalification.
claims.quote_verbatim: we would always have to make sure we had three different vendors and three different available parts that were qualified to go into the product so that we can actually swap them out if we needed to
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Where a device family spans graded variants, such as the 1N4004 through 1N4007 rectifiers differing only in voltage rating, listing every acceptable member against one BOM line lets any of them be fitted interchangeably.
claims.quote_verbatim: So you'd have all of those in your bomb. So at any point you could use, you can substitute in any of those and it'll work.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Package and packaging suffixes on a shared base part number are treated by buyers as the same item, but a change of base part number is not, so an acceptable alternate with a different base number must be explicitly called out on the BOM as a valid replacement.
claims.quote_verbatim: But when you actually change the base number, you know, a buyer is going to be like, well, that doesn't look the same. And so you have to specifically call that out
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Scraping distributor stock and grouping it by manufacturer during a shortage showed supply was highly uneven between vendors, with Microchip holding by a wide margin the most parts in stock.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was basically like scraping DigiKey and saying like, what's there?
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Hands-off quick-turn assembly services in the United States can deliver assembled boards in under a week at a substantial price premium, but only if the components on the BOM are themselves available.
claims.quote_verbatim: you could probably get it in less than a week, assuming your parts are available
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: When a mainstream part such as the CP2102 USB bridge is stripped from distributor stock, clone versions from Asian suppliers remain obtainable at low prices, which trades supply certainty against unverified provenance.
claims.quote_verbatim: Yeah, but these are the ones you can get all those Asian clones of. That's right. This is how you can get it for $2 delivered.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Fab capacity announced during a shortage takes roughly two to three years to come online, so publicly funded expansion offers no relief to a current sourcing crunch and may arrive into an oversupplied market.
claims.quote_verbatim: there will be apparently new chip fabs in about two to three years
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Best way to find a leak

claims.claim_text: New leading-edge fabs do not relieve shortages of the commodity analog and power parts most designs depend on, because those fabs are not built to produce simple devices such as voltage regulators.
claims.quote_verbatim: Intel ain't making your, uh, little, uh, voltage regulator
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Best way to find a leak

claims.claim_text: Supply during the 2020s shortage was concentrated by vendor to the point that some manufacturers' catalogues were effectively absent from distribution for years at a time.
claims.quote_verbatim: And I actually haven't seen any TI stuff in stock in the last three years.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Distributors will accept orders and payment for parts they cannot actually deliver, refunding the money later, so an accepted order is not evidence that stock exists.
claims.quote_verbatim: And if they can't, they'll simply refund your money. Right? These are vapor chips.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: During the 2021 shortage, parts ordered for a production run could fail to arrive for over a year; an instrument build stalled on an NXP device and an STM32F0 ordered in March or April 2021 that had still not been delivered, exhausting the product's supply.
claims.quote_verbatim: I ordered them in March or April of 2021, and they still haven't arrived.
claims.speaker: Matt Liberty
claims.episode_title: The Joulescope Upgrade with Matt Liberty

claims.claim_text: One response to extreme lead times is to order components for a product roughly a year ahead of production, before the design is even finalised, committing cash to inventory against a prototype that is still changing.
claims.quote_verbatim: So I started ordering parts for the JS220 in June or July of last year.
claims.speaker: Matt Liberty
claims.episode_title: The Joulescope Upgrade with Matt Liberty

claims.claim_text: The RP2040 remained purchasable in quantities of 500 through the shortage, which made availability itself a selection argument for the part.
claims.quote_verbatim: No, I went out and actually bought 500 and, you know, could buy 500.
claims.episode_title: The Joulescope Upgrade with Matt Liberty

claims.claim_text: Supply disruption hits consumables and mechanical items as hard as semiconductors: ESD foam sold through a distributor rose from about $20 to about $57 per sheet with shipping cost roughly doubling, a per-kit increase large enough to threaten a small kit business.
claims.quote_verbatim: That same sheet is now, like, $57 for that same sheet.
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: The parts that endanger a small hardware business during a shortage are often not the microcontrollers or passives but overlooked items such as packaging materials and specialist components like Geiger tubes that depend on a single import channel.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's actually not the resistors. It's not the microcontrollers, although you'd think.
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: Component sourcing consumes a growing share of a small manufacturer's operating time during a shortage, adding a labour cost on top of the higher component prices themselves.
claims.quote_verbatim: I spend so much time now dealing with component availability.
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: Optimising a design involves simultaneous pressure from cost, power, package and availability, so part selection cannot be reduced to a single objective.
claims.quote_verbatim: There's cost. I was also thinking about. There's availability. There's package.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Distributor search tools do not let a user rank the whole catalogue by stock quantity; availability sorting works only within a product category, so finding the most-stocked part overall requires category-by-category inspection.
claims.quote_verbatim: Can you actually sort by the most, the highest availability part? Well, you'd have to go through each category.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Defensive pre-buying during a shortage inflates the demand signal semiconductor vendors see, so order books overstate real consumption and the correction arrives as oversupply and cancelled forecasts once buyers' inventories are filled.
claims.quote_verbatim: Cause everybody's pre-buying and being like, Oh, we need all these parts. And then when it's time for delivery a couple of hours later and things have leveled out, it's like, Oh, actually we're coming back down to earth.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The semiconductor supply cycle reversed after the shortage, moving from scarcity to oversupply within a few years, with some component categories still constrained while the market overall loosened.
claims.quote_verbatim: In fact, there's an oversupply. That's right. Exactly. It's swung.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Laying out several alternative footprints for op amps and memory devices on the same board, so that whichever device is obtainable can be fitted, is a design-for-availability technique that pandemic-era shortages made relevant again.
claims.quote_verbatim: I remember doing designs where multiple, you know, opems were used, multiple memory footprints were used in order to make sure that whichever is going to be available, we are going to use it.
claims.speaker: Pallav Aggarwal

claims.claim_text: Low-cost assembly services that fit their own stocked components force the BOM to be reworked for each build, because the same part numbers cannot be relied on to be in the house catalogue months later.
claims.quote_verbatim: I can't get the same parts. Yeah. I have to redo the bomb basically each and every time because of that.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: An export plugin for the EDA tool that formats the BOM to the assembler's specification and checks each line against the assembler's parts database moves the availability check into the design environment.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's just like an export plugin for key CAD, which is great. It basically just kind of spits everything out, pre-formatted exactly how they want it, you know, checks it against their database
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: House stock at an assembly service is a live figure that another customer can exhaust in a single order, so a part shown as available while a design is in progress can disappear before the build is submitted.
claims.quote_verbatim: Oh, some bastard just bought 10,000, just cleaned them out.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
